newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sets out agenda for national security team.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sets out agenda for national security team.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said his new national security team would focus on curbing nuclear proliferation and post-Cold War security threats like terrorism, while promoting free trade and economic growth.

Clinton said he had a clear vision for the new team, which is to include U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright as Secretary of State and national security adviser Anthony Lake as director of the Central Intelligence Agency.

"I think we've got a clear vision ... At the end of the Cold War, going into a world which is a global village, what do we have to do to enhance the security of the American people? We have to finish the unfinished business of the Cold War," Clinton said in an interview with C-SPAN aired on Sunday night. The interview was taped on Dec. 9
Clinton's recent Cabinet appointments were welcomed by lawmakers, but many observers said the new national security team lacked a clear vision.

In addition to continuing negotiations with Russia on dismantling both countries' nuclear arsenals, the new team would have to deal with "the new security threats of the 21st century, especially enhanced terrorism, proliferation of weapons, including biological and chemical weapons," he said.

"And then we have to create a system of cooperation where nations share more of the burdens and responsibilities," Clinton said, citing as examples peace-keeping efforts coordinated within NATO, and U.N. involvement in the Gulf War.

Finally, the team would have to focus on creating "a global economic system that is more open and more expansive and gives more countries a chance to participate in the economic growth in a way that is also fair to countries like the United States, which have kept our markets open," he said.

Clinton said his second inaugural speech would be a "little longer" than the first, which was the third shortest inaugural address ever given by a president, behind George Washington's second and Abraham Lincoln's second.

But Clinton joked that it would not be too long, noting that President Harrison died of a cold a month after giving the longest inaugural speech on record, because he stayed out and gave such a long speech.
"For the health of the republic and the president, you probably ought to give a short speech," he said with a laugh.
Clinton, echoing his campaign theme of "building a bridge to the 21st century," said he would try to map out what was needed for America to move into the next century.

"I think it's ... important to get people to take a longer view and understand these four years in terms of how we are going to get into the 21st century with all of our people having a chance and with the country coming together and still being able to lead the world," he said.
